Guide

How to read the daily stock report

The US and Taiwan reports use the same layout. This guide goes through it from top to bottom and says what each part can and cannot tell you.

Start with the time stamp

Every report page opens with three facts: the trading session it describes, the time the report was generated, and whether that was before or after the market closed. Read them first. The US report is published while New York is still trading, so its prices are the latest available at that moment and can differ from the final close. The Taiwan report is finalised after the 13:30 Taipei close, and its institutional-flow figures arrive later still, so the newest Taiwan revision of a session is often generated the following morning.

The short code after "source payload" is the first twelve characters of a hash of the report data. Two pages with the same code were built from identical data.

Market regime

The regime is a one-word summary of the backdrop: risk-on, risk-off, neutral or mixed. It is produced by a fixed rule from three inputs: where the benchmark (SPY for the US, the TAIEX for Taiwan) sits against its 50-day and 200-day averages, how volatile the benchmark's daily returns have been over 20 sessions, and breadth.

Treat it as context for everything below it. A stock that looks strong in a risk-off report is swimming against the tide; the same reading in a risk-on report is moving with it. The regime does not say what happens next. It says which conditions held when the report was built. The exact thresholds are in how DappGo computes its signals.

Breadth

Breadth answers a simple question: is the move shared? The report gives it in two ways.

  • Share above the 20-day average. The percentage of tracked tickers priced above their own 20-day moving average. This is the breadth figure the regime rule uses. Below 30% is weak; above 55% is strong.
  • Advancers and decliners. How many tickers rose and fell on the day, with the median move. The median is more honest than an average here because one stock moving 20% cannot drag it.

The two can disagree, and the disagreement is informative. A day with many advancers but few names above the 20-day average is a bounce inside a decline. A day with many decliners while most names remain above the average is a pause inside an advance.

Sector table

Each row averages the one-day move and the 14-day RSI of the tracked tickers in that sector and attaches a temperature from Cold to Hot. Two cautions apply. First, a sector with one or two tracked names is really a statement about those names, which is why the summary text compares only sectors with at least two. Second, the table describes the tracked universe, not the whole market: the US list is a reviewed watchlist of 36 large names, and the Taiwan list is the 100 largest companies plus one ETF.

Largest moves

The movers tables show the five largest gains and losses with the 5-day and 30-day changes beside them. Read across the row. A stock up 4% today and down 25% over 30 days is a different situation from one up 4% today and up 25% over 30 days, though both appear in the same table.

Momentum extremes

This section lists tickers whose 14-day RSI is at or below 30, or at or above 70, with the distance of the price from its 20-day average and its position inside the 52-week range. An RSI below 30 means selling has dominated the last fourteen sessions. It is often called oversold, which suggests a rebound is due. It is not due. In a persistent decline RSI can stay under 30 for weeks. Use the list to find where pressure is concentrated, then look at the 52-week position to see whether the stock is near the bottom of its range or simply cooling off near the top.

Mean-reversion screen

The screen names up to three tickers that meet all of four conditions at once: price below the 20-day average, RSI between 30 and 55, a first sign of momentum turning up, and volatility that is not high relative to the rest of the universe. It then ranks the matches by a score. The page prints the conditions each match met.

A match is a description of a set-up that some traders look for. It is not a recommendation, it takes no account of your circumstances, and on many days nothing qualifies. When the list is empty the page says so.

What the Taiwan report adds

Taiwan publishes daily net buying and selling by three institutional groups: foreign investors, investment trusts and dealers. The report sums them over five sessions, in lots of 1,000 shares, and the archive page shows the largest foreign net buys and sells with the trust figure beside each. When foreign investors and trusts are on opposite sides of the same stock, price tends to be contested rather than trending.

What the US report adds

The US page lists tracked companies with an earnings date in the next 14 days. Earnings are the most common reason for a gap that no indicator anticipates, so check this table before reading anything into a quiet chart.

What the report does not do

It does not forecast prices, it does not know your holdings or your tolerance for loss, and it covers a fixed list of tickers. Its job is to measure the same things the same way every session so that changes stand out. The archive exists so you can check any reading against the sessions before it.
